content: The cervix, derived from the Latin word for neck, is the lower, narrow portion of the uterus that connects to the upper end of the vagina. It is cylindrical or conical in shape and protrudes through the upper anterior vaginal wall. Approximately half of its length is visible with appropriate medical equipment, while the remainder lies above the vagina and is not directly visible. It is sometimes referred to as the cervix uteri or the neck of the uterus. Anatomy Ectocervix The portion of the cervix that projects into the vagina is called the ectocervix or portio vaginalis. It is approximately 5 cm wide and has a convex, elliptical surface. The ectocervix is divided into anterior and posterior lips. External Os The opening of the ectocervix is known as the external os. The size and shape of the external os and the ectocervix vary significantly depending on age, hormonal state, and whether the woman has had a vaginal birth. In women who have not had a vaginal birth, the external os appears as a small, circular opening. In women who have had a vaginal birth, the ectocervix becomes bulkier, and the external os appears wider, more slit-like, and gaping. Endocervical Canal The passageway between the external os and the uterine cavity is called the endocervical canal. Its length and width vary widely, as does the overall size of the cervix. Flattened from anterior to posterior, the endocervical canal measures 7 to 8 mm at its widest point in women of reproductive age. Internal Os The endocervical canal terminates at the internal os, which is the opening of the cervix into the uterine cavity. Cervical Crypts The lining of the cervix contains pockets known as cervical crypts, which are responsible for producing cervical fluid. Histology The epithelium of the cervix consists of nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium at the ectocervix and simple columnar epithelium at the cervical canal. At certain times in life, the columnar epithelium is replaced by metaplastic squamous epithelium, forming what is known as the transformation zone. Nabothian cysts are commonly found in the cervix. Cervical Mucus After menstruation, the external os is blocked by thick, acidic mucus, which is considered infertile and prevents sperm from entering the uterus. Around ovulation, fertile mucus is produced, which has a higher water content, is less acidic, and exhibits a ferning pattern under low magnification. This ferning pattern, a branching structure, helps guide sperm through the cervix. Fertility awareness methods often involve observing changes in cervical mucus, such as its sensation at the vulva, elasticity (spinnbarkeit), transparency, and the presence of ferning. Hormonal contraceptives primarily prevent ovulation but also increase effectiveness by inhibiting the production of fertile cervical mucus. Conversely, methods to thin cervical mucus, such as taking guaifenesin before ovulation, may aid in achieving pregnancy. During pregnancy, the cervix is sealed by a special antibacterial mucosal plug, which prevents infection. This mucus plug is expelled as the cervix dilates during labor or shortly before. Cervical Position After menstruation and under the influence of estrogen, the cervix undergoes changes in position and texture: For most of the menstrual cycle, the cervix remains firm, similar to the tip of the nose, and is positioned low and closed. As ovulation approaches, the cervix becomes softer, rises, and opens in response to high estrogen levels. These changes, along with the production of fertile cervical mucus, support sperm survival and movement. Functionality During menstruation, the cervix stretches slightly to allow the shedding of the endometrium. This stretching is thought to contribute to the cramping pain experienced by many women. Evidence for this includes the observation that some women’s cramps diminish or disappear after their first vaginal birth, as the cervical opening widens. During childbirth, uterine contractions dilate the cervix up to 10 cm in diameter to allow the fetus to pass through. During orgasm, the cervix convulses, and the external os dilates. Dr. R. Robin Baker and Dr. Mark A. Bellis from the University of Manchester proposed that this behavior may draw semen into the uterus, increasing the likelihood of conception. However, later researchers, including Elisabeth A. Lloyd, have questioned the logic and experimental data supporting this theory. Cervical Cancer The cervix can be affected by cervical cancer, a specific type of cancer detectable through cytological examination of epithelial cells obtained via a Pap smear. Evidence indicates that exposure to human papillomavirus (HPV) increases the risk of cervical cancer. HPV is related to the viruses that cause warts. In 2004, the incidence of new cervical cancer cases in the United States was observed to be 7 per 100,000 women. Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Cervix The lymphatic drainage of the cervix follows the uterine arteries and cardinal ligaments to the parametrial, external iliac, internal iliac, obturator, and presacral lymph nodes. From these pelvic lymph nodes, drainage proceeds to the para-aortic lymph nodes. In some women, the lymphatics drain directly to the para-aortic nodes.
